cue: The centre is magnified, and the picture runs slowly, then jumps ahead.
rows: Eagles see more than twice as much detail as people do. A phone camera can’t capture that much detail, so this view magnifies the centre to suggest it.

A peregrine falcon can see a light flicker up to 129 times a second, and a Harris’s hawk up to 77. People see flicker up to 50 or 60 times a second. This view runs slowly and then jumps ahead to suggest the difference.
This view keeps the field of view your camera gives.

fov.note: the middle of a Cooper's hawk's 300 degrees and a short-toed eagle's 260 degrees, close to 360 minus a red-tailed hawk's 82 degree blind area

cpd.note: a Harris's hawk resolved 62.3 cycles per degree, above the highest value the engine takes, so the value sits at that ceiling, inside the 27.4 to 60 behavioral range of the same hawk

topoA.note: one round sharp middle stands in for the two foveas of each eye

fall.note: how fast sharpness falls away from the middle; no record gives it

rate.note: 60 divided by a Harris's hawk's flicker fusion of 77.7 hertz

sat.note: four kinds of single cone, so no muting of color

blindAt.note: the blind area lies above and at the rear of the head

blindDeg.note: the middle of 60 degrees for a Cooper's hawk and 82 degrees for a red-tailed hawk

blindSoft.note: how softly the edge of the blind area fades

rows: If you are a Harris's hawk, you can pick out black and white stripes as fine as 62.3 cycles per degree. Red and green stripes of equal brightness blur together sooner, at 21.6 cycles per degree.

A black kite resolved 25.9 to 32.7 cycles per degree and a Harris's hawk 27.4 to 60. A wedge-tailed eagle resolved 138 and a falcon in an older test 160. No single figure fits every hawk, eagle and falcon, so 40 is a choice inside the Harris's hawk range.
If you are a red-tailed hawk, each of your eyes has two foveas, small pits where sight is sharpest. A peregrine turns its head about 40 degrees to bring prey onto the deep fovea of one eye.

A Cooper's hawk's eyes together cover about 300 degrees, with a blind area of about 60 degrees, and a short-toed eagle's cover 260. A red-tailed hawk's blind area above and behind the head is about 82 degrees. You very likely see about 280 degrees around you, blind in a wedge of about 70 degrees above and behind your head.

If you are an American kestrel, your eyes move only about 1 degree in their sockets, and a Cooper's hawk's move about 8. Hawks and falcons move the head about every 2 seconds on average, and bald eagles about every 5. You very likely look at one place for 2 to 5 seconds before the next head move.
A Harris's hawk sees flicker up to 77.7 times a second, a saker falcon 102 and a peregrine 124.5. You very likely follow movement in finer steps than a human does.

Raptors very likely have four kinds of single cone, and the short-wave one is tuned to violet. In a peregrine and a common buzzard its pigment peaks near 405 nanometers. Colored oil droplets sit in the other three kinds.

Nobody has measured how sharpness falls from the center of your sight to its edge, or how your two foveas blend into one sharp middle. Where your blind wedge begins and how softly its edge fades are also unmeasured. The records give no pupil shape, no depth of focus and no peaks for the other three color pigments.
trial.note_compiled: The draft's gaze block was left out: it gave timings with no zone for the gaze to move, so nothing would jump.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: If you are a red-tailed hawk, you read about 17 cycles a degree, a little over half of the 30 a human reads on an eye chart. Only a few other hawks, eagles, falcons and vultures have been measured, and their figures differ widely from species to species. If yours is not one of them, nobody has measured how sharply you see.
rows.note: Left out the 160 cycles a degree (R13) and the eagle and Egyptian vulture figures (R2, R4) because they belong to other species or have no named hawk. Nothing on interreceptor angle was recorded.

rows.title: Speed
rows.text: If you are a peregrine falcon, you can see a light flicker even when it flashes at least 125 times a second, and a saker falcon sees it at about 100, where a human stops seeing flicker at about 60. If you are a Harris's hawk, the figure is about 80. Nobody has measured how fast you see in any other hawk, eagle or falcon.
rows.note: Left out a carried claim for other Falco species, since numbers may not travel between species.

rows.title: Field of view
rows.text: Straight ahead of you is a wedge that both eyes see at once. If you are a red-tailed hawk or an American kestrel, that wedge is about 35 degrees wide, and if you are a bald eagle, it is about 40. For most hawks, eagles and falcons nobody has measured how much of the full circle your two eyes take in together.
rows.note: Left out total field widths (R2 278, R30 300): their quotes give blind areas, not those values.
